intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RAPSN gene (601592) on chromosome 11p11.2.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not state the chromosomal location; accepted as standard nomenclature restating the gene.

paragraphs.text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11) is an autosomal recessive disorder of neuromuscular transmission caused by deficiency of rapsyn, a 43-kD postsynaptic protein that is essential for clustering acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the endplate. The result is endplate AChR deficiency (Ohno et al., 2002). Most patients present in the first year of life and a few present later. Nearly one-third have arthrogryposis at birth, and intercurrent infections or fever can trigger respiratory crises (Engel et al., 2015). Burke et al. (2003) distinguished an early-onset form and a late-onset form, the latter beginning in adolescence or adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Goldhammer et al. (1990) described 14 Jewish patients from 10 families of Iraqi or Iranian origin who had congenital myasthenia and facial malformations. The malformations were an elongated face, mandibular prognathism with class III malocclusion, and a high-arched palate. Muscle weakness was mainly limited to ptosis, weakness of the facial and masticatory muscles, and fatigable speech. The course was mild and nonprogressive.

paragraphs.text: Menold et al. (1998) studied 5 families of Iranian Jewish origin with 6 affected individuals who had been diagnosed with a phenotypically unique form of congenital myasthenic syndrome. Four of the families were consanguineous, and all came from the same geographic region. For this reason the authors considered it highly likely that the families carried the same ancestral CMS mutation.

paragraphs.text: Das et al. (2014) reported a 20-month-old boy with rapsyn deficiency. At birth he had a weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures and facial deformity. Because of respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue, he spent 71 days in the neonatal intensive care unit and 47 days in the pediatric intensive care unit. Imaging, metabolic and electrodiagnostic studies were normal. Muscle biopsy showed myofiber atrophy in a pattern consistent with early denervation.

paragraphs.text: In a review, Engel et al. (2015) stated that most patients with CMS due to rapsyn deficiency present in the first year of life, while a few present later. paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2002) studied 4 patients with CMS and endplate AChR deficiency who had no mutations in the AChR subunit genes. In these patients they identified 3 recessive mutations in the RAPSN gene, and all 4 patients carried the N88K mutation. Two patients were homozygous for N88K, which lies in tetratricopeptide repeat 3 (TPR3). One patient was compound heterozygous for N88K and L14P, which lies in TPR1. The fourth patient was compound heterozygous for N88K and a 553ins5 insertion that causes a frameshift in TPR5. In expression studies in HEK cells, none of the 3 mutations impaired rapsyn self-association, but all 3 reduced coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified 2 mutations in E-box elements of the RAPSN promoter region in 8 patients with CMS. Patient 1 carried a -27C-G mutation, and the allele carrying this mutation was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. Patients 2 through 8, who were Oriental Jews of Iraqi or Iranian origin, carried a -38A-G mutation. In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, -38A-G gained binding affinity, and -27C-G lost binding affinity, for different components of nuclear extracts from C2C12 myotubes. Both mutations reduced reporter expression in C2C12 myotubes. The authors concluded that impaired transcription from the RAPSN promoter predicts reduced rapsyn expression and AChR deficiency at the endplate, and they noted that these were the first E-box mutations reported.

paragraphs.text: Gaudon et al. (2010) described 3 patients with a characteristic phenotype of recessive CMS and a mutation in the RAPSN gene. Family analysis showed that direct sequencing had missed one mutant allele in each patient. Allelic quantification of the patients' DNA identified 3 novel multiexon deletions of RAPSN. paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a -38A-G mutation in the RAPSN promoter region in 7 patients with CMS (patients 2-8). The patients were Oriental Jews of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations. The mutation changes an E-box at -40 to -35 from CAACTG to CAGCTG without altering the consensus CANNTG sequence. In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, the mutation gained binding affinity for components of C2C12 myotube nuclear extracts, and it reduced reporter expression in C2C12 myotubes. Haplotype analysis showed that the mutation arose from a common founder.

paragraphs.text: Engel et al. (2015) stated that Near-Eastern Jewish patients homozygous for the c.-38A>G E-box mutation have a mild phenotype with ptosis, prognathism, severe weakness of the masticatory and facial muscles, and hypernasal speech.
